newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal government crisis appears near resolution.
newsitem.headline: Nepal government crisis appears near resolution.

text.p: Nepal's four-day-old political crisis appeared to be nearing an end on Monday after the party heading the outgoing coalition said it had failed to win new support and pulled out of the race to form a new government.

Nepali Congress party officials said prime minister Sher Bahadur Deuba, who resigned last Thursday after losing a confidence vote, would sit in the opposition after failing to cobble together a new coalition.

The announcement cleared the way for Lokendra Bahadur Chand of the centrist Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), who has already staked his claim, to be invited by King Birendra to form the next government of the Himalayan kingdom.
The king, who abandoned his absolute powers in 1990 but remains a constitutional monarch, has given the politicians until 6.00 p.m. (1215 GMT) to stake a claim to power.
Authorities said he could ask Chand immediately after that to form a new government.
The Nepali Congress officials said the party had failed to secure the RPP's support for a new coalition.
"We wanted to have a coalition on the party basis (with the entire RPP) not on an individual basis," said Lakshman Prasad Ghimire, chief secretary of the Nepali Congress.

He told Reuters that some RPP members wanted to form a coalition with the Nepali Congress while another RPP faction had supported Chand as prime minister. "Naturally we opt to sit in the opposition," Ghimire said.
Chand has the support of Nepal's former ruling communist party, the Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party.
Earlier on Monday UML General Secretary Madhav Kumar Nepal and Chand registered a joint claim to govern at the gates of King Birendra's palace.
The communist and RPP leaders were accompanied by Gajendra Narayan Singh, leader of the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP).
Both the RPP and NSP had supported the government, led by the centrist Nepali Congress, that resigned last week after losing a confidence vote in the lower house of parliament.

The UML leader told Reuters outside the palace that his party and its allies controlled 103 of 205 seats in the lower house of parliament -- just enough to survive -- and would support the RPP's Chand as the new prime minister.
"We have produced 103 signatures supporting Chand," Nepal said.
Deuba's three-party coalition took over in September 1995 from the communist UML, which ruled at the head of a minority government following inconclusive polls in 1994.
Squabbling among the three ruling parties undercut Deuba's coalition and led to the defection last week of at least 10 of the RPP's 19 lawmakers to the communist side.

UML is the biggest single party in the House of Representatives with 90 votes. It can count on 10 RPP votes, the NSP's two votes and one vote belonging to the communist Nepal Workers and Peasants Party (NWPP), UML sources said.
The Nepali Congress has 87 seats, but two of its lawmakers abstained in the test vote last week.

Chand was twice prime minister under the Panchayat system of government which lasted from 1961 until 1990 and permitted the king to rule directly over a partyless assembly in the world's only Hindu kingdom.
